content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Full memlint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural memlint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# Mac-Owned GPS/Perch/VALD Pulls and Sleep-Induced Lateness

On 2026-09-22 the three Baylor athlete-data pulls — GPS (Catapult), Perch, and VALD — completed their first full day running from the Mac after being moved off the Windows laptop. All three exited 0 and carried data through 9/21, but two of the three finished roughly an hour late because the Mac was asleep at their scheduled time. The session's decision was to accept the lateness rather than force a wake, on the grounds that the data arrived and only its arrival time was unreliable.

## Key Points

- **Schedule:** GPS 10:00 / 16:30, Perch 10:05 / 16:35, VALD 10:10 / 16:40 — all three now Mac-owned.
- **Sleep, not the scripts, is the failure mode.** The Mac slept at 3:45 PM; GPS ran on time at 16:32, but Perch and VALD only crept forward during short background wakes and did not finish until ~17:36–17:39. Perch timed out twice before try 3 succeeded. This is the same root cause as the earlier 6:30 AM GPS problem.
- **Retries saved the run but do not make it reliable** — the correct framing is "late, not missing," and the revisit trigger was set accordingly: reconsider only if GPS data goes *missing*, not merely late.
- **The decision was to leave sleep alone (Option 2).** The enable/undo commands are recorded in `DataBase_GPS_Reporting/docs/STATUS.md`: `sudo pmset repeat wakeorpoweron MTWRFSU 16:28:00` to enable, `sudo pmset repeat cancel` to undo.
- **Windows VALD was already off.** The disabled step 1 in `refresh_all_data.bat` *is* the VALD step, and the Windows VALD pull had been broken since 8/2 — so the migration inherited a dead leg rather than duplicating a working one.
- **No alerts fired, so the Perch and VALD failure-alert paths remain unproven** — a successful-but-late run exercises neither the alert nor the absence of one.
- **Two writers would mean two mismatched databases**, so the Windows GPS writer was marked stopped (per Eric's report; not verifiable from the Mac).
- **The exposed VALD client secret was deliberately not rotated** — the repo is private and the pulls work; the deferral is recorded in `_INBOX/docs/STATUS.md`.

## Details

The substantive insight is that a scheduled job on a laptop has an execution precondition the scheduler does not enforce: the machine must be awake. macOS will grant short background wakes that let a long-running pull inch forward without ever giving it a contiguous window, which is why Perch timed out twice and both late jobs finished in a ragged ~17:36–17:39 cluster rather than at a clean retry boundary. From the outside, every observable signal is healthy — exit code 0, data current to 9/21, retries doing their job — and only the timestamp reveals that the schedule is not actually being honored. This is the same shape as the `Ready`-forever triggerless task in [[concepts/windows-backup-task-trigger-gotchas]] and the sleeping-laptop-misses-fixed-time-trigger gotcha recorded there: the scheduling layer reports truthfully about its own narrow predicate while the operational question (did this run when it was supposed to?) goes unanswered. The generalized version is catalogued in [[connections/the-execution-context-silently-edits-the-work-set]] — session lifetime, mount state, and now sleep state all shrink or delay what a run attempts without producing an error.

The decision to leave `pmset` alone is worth recording as a decision rather than an omission, because it comes with an explicit revisit trigger. Forcing a daily wake at 16:28 would make the afternoon pulls punctual at the cost of waking the machine every day for a job whose output is consumed the following morning anyway; lateness inside a single day is therefore not a defect in the consuming workflow. The condition that *would* justify the wake — data going missing rather than arriving late — is narrower and falsifiable, which keeps the deferral from decaying into an unexamined default. The undo command being stored alongside the enable command in the repo's own `STATUS.md` is the mechanism that makes the choice cheap to reverse.

Two ancillary findings deserve attention. First, the failure-alert paths for Perch and VALD have still never been exercised: a run that is late but ultimately successful produces no alert and therefore proves nothing about whether an alert would fire on a genuine failure. That leaves the alerting path in the same unverified state described in [[connections/alerting-path-must-not-share-the-monitored-systems-budget]] — untested alerting is indistinguishable from broken alerting. Second, the single-writer rule for the GPS database is a correctness constraint, not a tidiness preference: two machines writing the same database produce two divergent copies, and the Windows job being stopped is asserted rather than verified because the Mac has no way to inspect Windows' scheduler. The unused GPS database copy at `FA2026/_Mark_for_Deletion/gps_db_handoff_2026-09-21/` on Drive was queued for deletion for the same reason — a spare copy of a database is a future source of confusion about which one is authoritative.

# Connection: A Guard That Cannot Run Fails Open

## The Connection

The 2026-09-22 stack audit found the dcg safety hook dead on the Windows laptop — 913 failures, because Windows settings point at the Mac path `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg`. The same day's data-pull review found that the Perch and VALD failure-alert paths had still never fired and remain unproven. Both are protective mechanisms whose absence produces exactly the same observable signal as their success: silence.

## Key Insight

A guard and an alert are both defined by what they do in the bad case, which means neither is exercised by the good case. When such a mechanism is broken, the system does not degrade visibly — it degrades into looking fine. The operator's model still includes the protection, so the perceived risk drops precisely when the actual risk rises.

This inverts the usual debugging heuristic. For a productive component, absence of output is a symptom; for a protective component, absence of output is the expected steady state, and the only way to distinguish "working and quiet" from "dead and quiet" is to deliberately produce the condition it guards against — or, failing that, to check the mechanism's own liveness independently of its verdicts. The 913 failure records are what made the dcg case discoverable at all: the hook was loud about failing to run, and nobody was reading that channel. The Perch/VALD alerts have no such record, so their state is not merely unknown but unknowable from the outside.

The practical consequence is that a protective mechanism needs two things a productive one does not: a liveness signal separate from its findings, and a periodic deliberate trip. Neither is expensive. Both were absent here.

## Evidence

- **dcg on Windows:** 913 recorded failures from a Mac-absolute path in Windows settings; "the dcg guard checks nothing there." The guard was nominally configured in both places, and its configuration was the only thing anyone had checked.
- **Perch and VALD alerts:** "No alerts fired, so the Perch and VALD failure-alert paths are still unproven." The 2026-09-22 run was late but ultimately successful, so it exercised neither the alert nor a genuine no-alert case; the item was carried forward as "test the Perch/VALD failure alerts."
- **Precedent — the morning-briefing failure email** died because its send path used the same dead venv it was meant to report on, going six days undetected; and the `-DryRun` guard in `daily-backup.ps1` printed "committed / pushed" for operations it never performed, because the log line sat outside the guard it described.

# Connection: Verify Across Every Partition the Write Touched

## The Connection

Three checks on 2026-09-22 returned accurate answers to questions narrower than the ones being asked. The PFF snapshot load was verified by comparing the 2026 season and reported success while 12,750 rows had been deleted from 2024–2025. The Mac-owned data pulls were verified by exit code and data currency — both genuinely clean — while two of three jobs had run an hour off schedule. And the same day's earlier inventory verification, from the 2026-09-07 pattern, established the counter-example: it checked the raw `.xlsx`, compared md5s across two locations, *and* searched the whole home folder for a newer export before concluding nothing had changed.

## Key Insight

The scope of a verification is chosen, usually implicitly, by whatever is cheapest and most salient to sample — and salience runs exactly opposite to risk. The current season is the most visible partition and the one the operation was designed to get right; the historical seasons are invisible and are precisely where the two machines' holdings had silently diverged. A load that writes N partitions requires N checks, not one check on the partition you were thinking about.

The rule generalizes past row counts. "Partition" means any dimension along which the operation's effect varies: seasons in a database load, but also the *time* dimension for a scheduled job (exit code covers whether it ran, not when), and *location* for a file that exists in two places (a filename match is not a content match). In each case the narrow check is not wrong — it is true and insufficient, which is the dangerous combination, because a truthful pass is read as an all-clear.

The practical test is to state, before verifying, what the operation could have changed, and then confirm that the check's scope covers that set. The PFF load could have changed four tables across three seasons; the check covered one season. The pull could have changed data content *and* arrival time; the check covered content. Only the inventory verification enumerated its own possible-change surface first and then built three independent checks to span it.

## Evidence

- **PFF load (2026-09-22):** the first verification "said it worked — that was wrong. The first check only compared 2026, so it missed the loss." 12,750 Mac-only 2024–2025 `pff_premium` rows across `video_plays`, `team_play`, `quarterback_charting`, and `rushing` were silently deleted. Recorded lesson: "Row-count checks must cover every season the load touches."
- **Mac data pulls (2026-09-22):** all three pulls exited 0 with data current to 9/21 — a fully passing content check — while GPS ran on time and Perch/VALD finished ~17:36–17:39 against 16:35/16:40 schedules, Perch timing out twice first. The temporal partition was outside the check's scope.
- **Tech inventory (2026-09-07, the counter-example):** "has anything changed?" was answered by reading the raw `.xlsx` rather than the cleaned CSV, comparing local and OneDrive copies by md5 rather than filename, and searching the home folder for a newer export — three checks spanning content, replication, and existence. That breadth is what exposed the Microsoft-Forms-versus-Google-Forms drift, which no single check would have surfaced.

# Windows Laptop Backup Failure and RECOVERY-INVENTORY.md

On 2026-09-14 a `RECOVERY-INVENTORY.md` commit arriving from the Windows laptop revealed that the machine had **no working backup at all**. Roughly 15 GB exists in a single copy only — `SportScienceResearchRepo` (4.37 GB), `Football` (2.94 GB), `Risk_Stratification_Engine` (1.80 GB), `ForcePlate_DecisionSystem` (1.69 GB), and the `~/.codex` history. Everything else — all 131 repos, `~/.claude`, skills, global memory, and Google Drive documents — is safe. The failure had three independent root causes, all of them artifacts of the Mac migration.

## Key Points

- **Nine KeystoneOS Windows scheduled tasks are Disabled** — switched off during the move to the Mac and never restored. They report their disabled state accurately; nothing ever escalated it.
- **Two replacement tasks were registered with no trigger.** A triggerless task shows `Ready` indefinitely and will never fire — the healthiest-looking possible state for a job that does nothing.
- **The Windows backup manifest is the Mac's manifest.** It carries `/Volumes/CRASHBOX` and `/Users/kristinarash/...` paths, with its last state written 2026-08-14 at status ERROR. `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` had likewise been overwritten by the Mac version (rsync + Mac paths) on 2026-08-05; the original is frozen at `daily-backup.ps1.win-orig`.
- **`backup_dev.ps1` was changed from `/MIR` to `/E`.** Mirroring propagates accidental deletions into the backup, which converts the backup into a second copy of a mistake rather than a recovery path. (`backup_ai_sessions.ps1` was already `/E`.)
- **Two deliberate non-actions:** the backup scripts stay in `DEV\_INBOX\` because the registered scheduled task points there, and the nine disabled tasks are *not* re-enabled because the script they invoke is now the Mac's.

## Details

What makes this a distinct failure rather than another manifest-drift instance is that every layer reported truthfully and none of them reported the operational fact. A disabled task is disabled; a triggerless task is genuinely ready; a manifest containing Mac paths is a syntactically valid manifest. The only signal that would have surfaced the problem is the one nobody was checking: whether bytes actually landed in Google Drive. This is the same scope mismatch catalogued in [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]], where `launchctl list` reports only the last *scheduled* run — the field answers a narrower predicate than the operator's question and is therefore silent about the gap. The recovery report's own conclusion states the rule directly: verification must confirm bytes at the destination, not that the task looks healthy.

The three causes also share a single origin. Tasks disabled "during the Mac move," a manifest overwritten with Mac paths on 08-14, a `daily-backup.ps1` overwritten on 08-05 — the migration edited the Windows machine's automation surface as a side effect of syncing shared files, and nothing on the Windows side was left running to notice. This extends the pattern in [[connections/windows-defaults-outlive-the-windows-machine]] in the opposite direction: that article covers Windows assumptions surviving onto the Mac, whereas here Mac-shaped configuration flowed back onto Windows through the same shared repositories. Bidirectional sync between two machines with platform-specific automation means any file that encodes host facts — paths, mount points, shell dialects — is a collision waiting to happen, which is why the new `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.windows.json` was created as a *separate* file rather than a re-edit of the shared one.

The `/MIR` → `/E` change deserves isolation as policy. Robocopy's `/MIR` makes the destination an exact mirror of the source, which means a local deletion is faithfully reproduced in the backup at the next run — the backup is then a copy of the current state rather than a record of history. `/E` copies without deleting, accepting stale files in exchange for never propagating a loss. The trade-off resolves the same way as the append-only forecast log in [[concepts/cross-machine-conflict-file-triage]]: when the artifact's value is that it holds something the source might no longer have, the correct verb is never "make identical."

# Machine-Restore Closeout and Handoff Note

The 2026-08-11 end-of-day session closed out a multi-day machine-restore checklist: an SSD backup baseline, a Zotero CLI/MCP bundle installation, cleanup of a failed-run artifact, and a written handoff note committed to the global-memory repository. The closeout distinguishes between items genuinely finished, items intentionally left to drain on their own schedule, and items deliberately parked.

## Key Points

- **Handoff artifact:** `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-08-06-restore-closeout.md`, committed and pushed — a durable, versioned record of restore state rather than a memory-tier entry.
- **Zotero MCP registered user-scope:** binary at `~/go/bin/zotero-research-library-pp-mcp`, registered as `zotero`; bundle at `~/printing-press/library/zotero-research-library/zotero-research-library.mcpb`.
- **Backup baseline closed:** first full `CRASHBOX` run completed clean (OK, 0 errors, 21:25).
- **Self-draining items are not blockers.** The compiler backlog of 54 daily logs drains on the nightly schedule; PR monitors for #1667 and #1668 were intentionally left stopped because the ball is on the maintainer's side.
- **Parked items carried forward unchanged:** `GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD`, Milvus, and skill-tax — the same three items parked during the 2026-08-06 loose-ends sweep, confirming they remain deliberate deferrals rather than forgotten work.

## Details

The closeout illustrates a three-way classification that keeps an end-of-day review honest. The first class is genuinely complete work with a verifiable artifact: the backup ran clean and produced a receipt, the MCP binary was registered and its bundle staged, and the handoff note was committed and pushed. The second class is work that is neither done nor blocking because a scheduled process will drain it without attention — the 54-log compiler backlog is the canonical example, since the nightly compile job consumes it incrementally, so listing it as an action item would misrepresent it as requiring human effort. The third class is work owned by someone else or explicitly deferred: PRs #1667 and #1668 sit with the maintainer, so the background monitors watching them were stopped rather than left running to generate noise.

The parked trio — `GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD`, Milvus, and skill-tax — is notable for having been carried unchanged since the 2026-08-06 sweep. Restating them at closeout rather than dropping them preserves the distinction between a deliberate deferral and an item that quietly fell off the list; a parked item that stops appearing in closeouts becomes indistinguishable from forgotten work. Routing the whole picture into a committed handoff file under `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` rather than into a memory tier reflects the same routing discipline documented elsewhere: durable state that already has a natural on-disk home should live there, with memory reserved for pointers and conventions. Stopping the PR monitors also aligns with the finding that background monitor events are unreliable — a monitor left running against work that cannot progress produces duplicate or spurious notifications rather than signal.

# SpeedProfiling Project (Baylor Football Velocity Profiling)

SpeedProfiling is a Baylor football velocity-profiling project that pulls full-game 10 Hz Catapult GPS data, aligns it with college football play-by-play (via CFBD / cfbfastR), and produces per-athlete speed/velocity profiles adapted from a workshop method authored by "Alex." The project is developed as a private R repository (`github.com/erash11/SpeedProfiling`, 176-package renv lockfile) executed against a 7-ticket implementation plan tracked in the KeystoneOS `.scratch/speedprofiling/issues/` directory, using the mattpocock `implement` and `code-review` skills. On 2026-07-18, tickets 01, 02, 04, and 07 were advanced; on 2026-07-20, ticket 05 (GPS↔play-by-play merge, on-field separation, workload tables) was closed and shipped on PR #3.

## Key Points

- **Ticket-driven, per-session workflow:** the project is decomposed into 7 tickets; each ticket is implemented in a fresh session via `/mattpocock-skills:implement <ticket path>`. The `Status:` line in each ticket file is the claim mechanism that prevents parallel-session collisions. Eric prefers fresh parallel sessions per ticket over driving all tickets from one session.
- **catapultR credentials-object API change:** the installed catapultR uses a new credentials-object API — `ofCloudCreateToken(sToken=…, sRegion='America')`; the old `token=` argument no longer exists. `R/01_get_data.R` was rewritten for this API in ticket 04.
- **Deleting a token file does not revoke it server-side:** the old 2023 Catapult token had to be revoked manually in the OpenField UI — removing the local JWT file does not invalidate the token on Catapult's servers. Ticket 02 hardened `.gitignore` against `AccessTokens.txt`/`*token*.txt` and migrated live values into `.Renviron`, but server-side revocation of a superseded token is a separate manual step (logged as an Eric-manual action item).
- **Full 10 Hz pull verified (ticket 04):** the pull retrieved 8,932,931 rows at true 10 Hz (0.1 s spacing, max velocity 20.3 mph) for all 61/61 athletes (79 MB, gitignored) plus 188 play-by-play plays; 69/69 testthat tests pass. A feasibility probe gate hard-stops before the bulk pull unless genuine 10 Hz rows with all required columns return.
- **Ticket 05 — GPS↔play-by-play alignment (2026-07-20):** merged 10 Hz GPS with play-by-play using the kickoff surge signature as a numerical time anchor, separated on-field from sideline athletes via a two-part rule (sideline boundary + metabolic-power gate), and produced per-play workload tables. Closed on PR #3. See [[concepts/speedprofiling-gps-playbyplay-alignment]].
- **Game selection is config, not code:** game selection moved from hardcoded `GAME_*` variables to a `GAMES` table in `R/config.R` (activity ID + cfbd args per row). Adding a game is a one-row config edit; an empty `GAMES` renders the activity list to pick from. Per-game `.rds` caching pays the slow pull once.
- **Stacked PRs merge in order #1 → #2 → #3;** ticket 04's PR #2 is stacked on ticket 03's PR #1.

## Details

The project adopts a set of workshop R scripts (from an author "Alex") as reference material and re-implements them ticket by ticket against Baylor's live data sources. Ticket 01 established the repo, adopted the Drive scripts/docs, and set FERPA rules in AGENTS.md with a CLAUDE.md adapter, gitignore protection, and a private repo. A standards review of the adopted scripts found four real defects — notably a timestamp-conversion bug in `01_get_data.R` and play-end windows in `02_combine_data.R` that erroneously absorb halftime gaps — which were logged to the tracker and mapped to downstream tickets 03–06 rather than patched twice in reference code. Ticket 02 decoded the Catapult JWT scopes (`connect, catapultr, sensor-read-only`, expiry 2126), confirming the sensor scope needed for the 10 Hz feasibility probe, and migrated tokens from an untracked `AccessTokens.txt` (hardened out via `.gitignore` patterns `AccessTokens.txt` and `*token*.txt`) into `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\.Renviron` (`CATAPULT_TOKEN`, `CFBD_API_KEY`). Two environment notes surfaced during setup: the local `G:\My Drive` mount is much faster for adopting workshop files than downloading them through the Drive API, and `reactablefmtr` was archived off CRAN so it must be installed from GitHub for a clean renv restore (the renv snapshot-type setting also had to be fixed for `renv::status()` to report clean).

Ticket 04 delivered the core game-data pull (8.9M rows at true 10 Hz for 61 athletes), verified end-to-end (69/69 tests, both `.rds` caches hit on re-run). The BYU game (BYU – G5 – 09.28.24) was auto-selected because ticket 02 had already verified its play-by-play and Eric was unavailable to pick interactively; swapping games is a one-row `GAMES` config edit. Ticket 04 anticipated two forward-looking findings for ticket 05: Catapult X/Y coordinates return in venue coordinates requiring a transform, and the cfbfastR `wallclock` column might simplify GPS↔play timestamp alignment. Ticket 05 (2026-07-20) resolved both — the venue-coordinate issue via PCA field-frame recovery and the timestamp alignment via the kickoff surge signature rather than `wallclock`. A recurring environment note: background R tasks can report a false "exit code 1" even when the script log shows a clean end-to-end run, so the log must be checked before assuming failure (see [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]). Ticket 03 (analysis core + tests) and ticket 07 (KeystoneOS/SecondBrain integration) were also run as parallel fresh sessions, and ticket 06 (velocity profiles — sprint detection, NLS fits, bootstrap CIs, position-group comparisons) remains downstream.

# KeystoneOS Repo Intake Flow (inventory → intake → promote)

The KeystoneOS repo intake flow is the AGENTS.md-defined three-stage pipeline — `inventory` → `intake` → `promote` — for discovering repositories across configured discovery roots and registering genuinely new ones in the KeystoneOS project registry. On 2026-07-13, a run scanned 58 candidates (14 already registered), promoted two genuinely new repos as "Active candidate," left 17 low-signal items in the review bucket, and committed the registry update under standing auto-commit authorization.

## Key Points

- **Three-stage flow:** `inventory` scans discovery roots for candidate repos; `intake` scores and buckets candidates, writing a report (`outputs/intake/2026-07-08-project-intake.md`); `promote` registers selected candidates in the registry. Each item in the intake report carries its own recommended promote command.
- **2026-07-13 results:** 58 candidates scanned, 14 already registered; two new repos promoted — `cmj_traffic_light` (CMJ recovery monitoring for Volleyball, 4 commits, registered at its OneDrive work-drive path as its only home) and `PlayerProfiles_FB_03_28_2026` (football player profiles with Perch API ingest, 43 commits, registered at canonical `DEV\` path). 17 low-signal items left unpromoted in the review bucket.
- **DEV is canonical; skip OneDrive shadows:** OneDrive INBOX copies of Travel_Map, ForcePlate_DecisionSystem, and PlayerProfiles were skipped as shadows of already-registered DEV repos, per drive-topology policy. A repo whose only home is OneDrive (cmj_traffic_light) is registered at that path; a repo with a canonical DEV copy is registered there and its OneDrive duplicate ignored.
- **Ambiguous scope flagged, not assumed:** the user's "new repo ingestion" phrasing was interpreted as discover-and-register-all-new, but the assistant flagged the assumption and offered to promote specific review-bucket repos instead if that was the intent.
- **JSON schema and PowerShell gotchas:** the intake report's JSON schemas differed from initial assumptions — inspect shapes before parsing and use the report's own recommended promote commands. PowerShell `Select-Object` clipped formatted `keystone.ps1 health` output; rerun `health` plain rather than piping through `Select-Object`.

## Details

The intake flow operationalizes the earlier DEV-sweep classification model (see [[concepts/keystoneos-project-registry]]) as a repeatable, command-driven pipeline. Where the DEV sweep bucketed projects into confirmed-live / ambiguous / inactive, the intake flow produces a scored candidate report and registers only genuinely new, sufficiently-signaled repos as "Active candidate," leaving low-signal items in a review bucket for explicit user decision. The conservatism is the same: ambiguous or low-signal repos are never auto-promoted, and the run flagged its own interpretation of an ambiguous user instruction rather than proceeding silently. The two promotions on 2026-07-13 illustrate the drive-topology policy in action — `cmj_traffic_light` was registered at its OneDrive path because that is its only home, while `PlayerProfiles_FB_03_28_2026` was registered at its canonical `DEV\` path and its OneDrive INBOX duplicate skipped, consistent with the rule that DEV is canonical and OneDrive copies are shadows.

Two operational gotchas surfaced. First, the intake report's JSON output did not match the shapes initially assumed for parsing; the correct practice is to inspect the actual JSON structure before writing parse logic and to use each item's own recommended promote command rather than reconstructing commands independently. Second, piping the formatted output of `keystone.ps1 health` through PowerShell's `Select-Object` clipped the display — a rendering artifact of PowerShell's formatted-object pipeline rather than a data problem — so the reliable path is to rerun `health` plain without the pipe. The registry update was committed and pushed to main (`7140ad1`) under the KeystoneOS repo's standing auto-commit authorization, and review-bucket candidates (e.g., AT_Utilization_Benchmarks, baylor-gps-football) remain unpromoted pending user direction.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]] — The AGENTS.md routing table that the project registry feeds; the intake flow is itself defined by AGENTS.md, making AGENTS.md both the routing surface and the process specification.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

## Evidence

- 2026-04-22 (10:57): "Background agent produced `docs/batch_r7_fixes.json` but hallucinated wrong author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358... Used PyPDF2 text extraction to verify actual authors and corrected all three citations before committing."
- 2026-04-22 (17:21): "Photo failed to render in localhost preview — identified as a server limitation (brainstorm preview server doesn't serve image files), not an HTML error... always verify photo rendering by opening the HTML directly in Chrome via file:// URL."

# Connection: Every Layer Reported Healthy Except the Destination

## The Connection

Three independent backup investigations converged on the same terminal check. On Windows, two replacement tasks showed `Ready` indefinitely because they had no trigger, nine others were `Disabled` and honest about it, and the manifest they consulted was syntactically valid — every layer answered correctly, and ~15 GB had no second copy. On the Mac, `status: OK` measured attempted jobs only, so a run with 9 of 31 jobs reported zero errors. And a restore test returned 57 of 61 skills from a backup whose own records showed nothing wrong, because the missing four sat behind a two-hop symlink into an unbacked-up vendor directory. In all three, the only question that discriminated was asked at the destination: are the bytes there?

## Key Insight

**Every status field in a backup pipeline reports on its own stage, and a chain of locally-truthful stage reports carries no information about end-to-end coverage.** This is stronger than "status fields can lie" — none of these fields lied. `Ready` correctly means not-running-and-not-disabled. `status: OK` correctly means no attempted job errored. A backup's manifest of what it copied correctly lists what it copied. The defect is compositional: each stage's predicate is narrower than "the data is recoverable," and narrowness does not aggregate into breadth no matter how many green stages are chained.

The practical consequence is that verification must *terminate* at the artifact, not at any report about the artifact — and the specific form that takes differs by what could go wrong upstream. Where the risk is that the job never ran, check that it produced output at the destination and that the schedule shows a real `NextRunTime` rather than a perpetual `Ready`. Where the risk is that the job ran over the wrong set, check cardinality — `okCount`, job count, entry count — against an expectation, since a null error set cannot be compared to anything. Where the risk is that the copy is unusable, restore it, because a backup that cannot be read back is indistinguishable from a backup that was never made.

The Windows case adds a corollary the Mac cases could not surface: a report can be healthy because the job is *absent from the reporting system entirely*. A disabled task emits no failures. A triggerless task emits no failures. An exclusion from a manifest emits, at best, an advisory. Absence is the quietest possible failure, and it is the one that a "check for errors" habit is structurally incapable of finding — which is why the counting checks and the destination checks are complements rather than alternatives.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-14: nine KeystoneOS Windows tasks `Disabled` since the Mac move, two replacements registered with no trigger showing `Ready` forever, and a Windows manifest containing only Mac paths — with the conclusion recorded that "verification must confirm bytes landed in Google Drive, not that the task looks healthy — that's the gap the whole recovery report traces back to."
- 2026-09-14: `G:` is a per-user mount, so a task running as SYSTEM "sees no `G:` and writes nothing, silently" — a successful-looking run that produced no output at the destination.
- 2026-09-09: `status: OK` established as measuring attempted jobs only, with `okCount` as the cross-check and the expected count itself moving 28 → 76 the same day.
- 2026-09-12: a restore test returned 57 of 61 skills, exposing a two-hop symlink chain into `~/.agents/vendor-review/` that the backup's own records could not have revealed.
- 2026-09-04: the `CAPTURE` and `STATE-SSD` job classes exist only when the SSD is mounted, so an unmounted drive produces a clean run over a silently smaller work set.

# Fix From the Working Machine, Hand the Broken One a Paste-Ready Page

Facing a broken Windows backup that could only be *repaired* on Windows, the 2026-09-14 session chose to do as much of the work as possible from the Mac: edit the scripts, author the new manifest, and write a single instruction page for the Windows machine to follow. The stated rationale was that the edits are safe to make from the Mac, and doing so converts the eventual Windows session from a debugging job into one paste.

## Key Points

- **The split is by what each machine can do, not by where the problem is.** File edits travel through the shared repos and were done on the Mac; only the operations that require the Windows machine's own scheduler (`Set-ScheduledTask`, admin PowerShell 7, a logged-in user session) were deferred.
- **The deliverable is an instruction page, not an executable.** The user asked twice for clarification on "the Windows file" — the wording was ambiguous about whether it was a script to run or a page to follow. Naming the artifact's *kind* is part of the handoff.
- **A file that nothing reads yet is documented as such.** `backup-manifest.windows.json` records the real Windows destinations, with an explicit note inside the file that no checker consumes it — it is documentation until a Windows checker exists.
- **Two constraints were recorded as prohibitions:** do not move the scripts out of `DEV\_INBOX\` (the registered task points there), and do not re-enable the nine disabled tasks (their script is now the Mac's version).
- **Deferring the fix to "next time I'm on Windows" was the rejected alternative,** because it would have carried the whole diagnosis into a future session that would have to re-derive it.

## Details

The move generalizes beyond this incident. When two machines share a repository, the class of work that can be performed remotely is larger than it first appears: anything that is a file edit — scripts, configuration, manifests, instructions — can be authored from whichever machine the operator is currently sitting at, because the sync layer delivers it. What genuinely cannot be done remotely is narrow and identifiable: operations against the other machine's OS-level state, its scheduler, its mounted volumes, its running processes. Partitioning the work along that line front-loads all the thinking into the session that has the context and leaves the other machine a mechanical checklist. This is the same economy as the ten-section `docs/WINDOWS-SYNC.md` queue in [[concepts/dev-thin-repo-github-consolidation]], where the shared repo became a work channel between two machines that share no filesystem.

The two documentation choices are what make the handoff durable rather than merely present. Writing "nothing reads this yet" *inside* `backup-manifest.windows.json` addresses the file's most likely future misreading — a maintainer finding a plausible manifest and assuming it is live, or finding it stale and assuming a checker broke. This is the same in-file rationale discipline that kept `CLAUDE.md` from being collapsed into an `@AGENTS.md` pointer, and that kept `DexaProject`'s permanent manifest warning from being repeatedly re-investigated: the explanation belongs in the file the next reader will open, not in a commit message. The two prohibitions serve the same function in reverse — they pre-empt the two most natural "tidying" impulses (move the scripts somewhere sensible; turn the disabled tasks back on), each of which would break something.

The repeated clarification request about "the Windows file" is a small but real lesson about handoff wording. A path handed across a machine boundary is ambiguous between several kinds of artifact — a script to execute, a document to read, a config to install — and the receiving side cannot disambiguate from the filename. Stating the kind and the verb ("follow this page"; "run this script") removes a round trip, which matters more when the receiving side is a future session or another agent rather than the same person minutes later.

# Morning Email Briefing System Design

On 2026-05-21, a design spec for an automated morning email briefing system was written and committed to `Desktop/DEV/morning-briefing/docs/2026-05-21-morning-briefing-design.md`. The system ingests email and calendar sources, distills them into a structured 6-section briefing, and delivers the result from Gmail to the user's work Outlook inbox at approximately 07:30 each morning. A durable markdown copy is saved to the SecondBrain vault regardless of delivery status. The implementation plan was started but not completed — the session hit its context-window limit mid-generation. On 2026-06-08, a full manual inbox audit validated the 6-section taxonomy against real Outlook inbox content, confirming the category distribution and the practical utility of separating FYI/newsletters from actionable sections.

## Key Points

- **Delivery config:** trigger at 07:20 so the briefing arrives ~07:30; send **from** `eric.rash11@gmail.com` **to** the user's work Outlook address (primary inbox). First-arrival junk-filter risk for Exchange tenants: `eric.rash11@gmail.com` should be added to safe-senders to prevent the first delivery being routed to junk by Exchange's external-sender heuristics.
- **6-section briefing format (all approved):** NEEDS REPLY, FOLLOW UPS, MEETINGS TO SCHEDULE, FORMS/TASKS OWED, STILL OPEN FROM PRIOR DAYS (age-tagged), FYI.
- **Live validation (2026-06-08):** a full manual Outlook inbox audit produced 50 categorized items: 11 needs_reply, 3 follow_ups, 3 meetings_to_schedule, 3 forms_owed, 6 still_open, 24 FYI/newsletters. The distribution confirms the design hypothesis — FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume (48%) but require no action, while actionable obligations are concentrated in a smaller set of items. See [[concepts/inbox-triage-methodology]].
- **No auto-learning:** the allowlist and mute list are manually curated only ("30 seconds a week"); automated pattern-learning was deliberately rejected to keep behavior predictable and auditable.
- **Graceful degradation:** the system must never silently skip a briefing — if a source fails, the briefing still sends with a banner explaining what could not be retrieved. Silent failures that leave the inbox empty are worse than a degraded briefing.
- **Durable markdown copy:** each day's briefing is saved to `Desktop/SecondBrain/morning-briefings/YYYY-MM-DD.md` regardless of email delivery outcome — the vault copy is a non-negotiable design requirement, not an optional log.
- **Self-review caught a spec gap:** a checklist self-review step during implementation plan generation identified that carryover items (STILL OPEN FROM PRIOR DAYS) were not being matched against today's new email threads for resolution detection — a behavioral omission in spec Section 8 that would have caused stale items to accumulate even after they were addressed in follow-up threads. The session hit the context-window limit while patching this gap, leaving the implementation plan incomplete.

## Details

The design spec's graceful-degradation principle is the most architecturally significant decision in the system. Making the briefing always send *something* — even a degraded version with a banner such as "⚠ Calendar source unavailable today" — is a conscious choice to prefer visible, annotated failures over silent ones. A pipeline that fails silently produces no signal that something broke; a degraded briefing with an explanatory banner tells the user what the system intended and why it could not fully deliver. This framing also means the implementation must treat each source (email, calendar, carryover state) as independently degradable — no single source failure should prevent the briefing from sending.

The self-review step during implementation plan generation caught a real behavioral defect in the spec before any code was written. The `writing-plans` skill includes a review checklist pass; that pass identified that the STILL OPEN section's carryover logic (spec Section 8) lacked a mechanism for detecting when a prior-day item had since been addressed by a new email thread — a gap that would have caused the carryover list to grow monotonically rather than shrinking as items were resolved. This is a planning-layer instance of the same principle documented in [[connections/multi-stage-review-catches-agent-blind-spots]]: a second review pass with a different focus (behavioral completeness rather than format compliance) catches what the initial drafting pass misses. Two items remain outstanding before implementation can proceed: the work Outlook email address (currently a placeholder in the spec), and completion of the implementation plan (left mid-write when the session expired).

The 2026-06-08 live inbox audit (see [[concepts/inbox-triage-methodology]]) validated the 6-section taxonomy against a real Outlook inbox. The distribution — 11 needs_reply, 3 follow_ups, 3 meetings_to_schedule, 3 forms_owed, 6 still_open, 24 FYI/newsletters — confirms that FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume (48%) but require no action, while actionable items are concentrated across the 5 actionable categories. This empirical validation supports the design decision to separate FYI from actionable sections rather than interleaving them. The same structured 6-category taxonomy drives both the manual triage process and this automated daily briefing, making the taxonomy the stable architectural element across both tools — see [[connections/inbox-triage-and-morning-briefing-taxonomy]].

# Skylar Zinnecker CMJ Return-to-Competition Reports

A series of CMJ (countermovement jump) force-plate performance reports were built for Baylor Athletics athlete Skylar Zinnecker on 2026-04-14, to support a return-to-competition (RTC) decision following injury and surgery. The reports were delivered as polished, print-ready HTML files using Chart.js, and were followed by a terminology cleanup and project documentation pass.

## Key Points

- Source data was a VALD ForceDecks export (`CMJ-test-export-04_14_2026.csv`, 67 sessions spanning August 2023-April 2026), processed into HTML reports with Chart.js visualizations.
- Injury (April 12, 2025) and surgery (April 25, 2025) dates were annotated as vertical markers on the charts.
