# Deferred Credential Rotation With a Recorded Rationale (VALD Client Secret)

During the 2026-09-21 closeout of the Windows→Mac data-pull cutover, an exposed VALD client secret was found and deliberately not rotated. The stated reasoning was that the repository holding it is private and the pulls are working; the choice was written into `_INBOX/docs/STATUS.md` as "skip for now" rather than left as an unrecorded omission. The deferral is defensible on its own terms but is notably weaker than the same day's `pmset` deferral, because no condition was named that would trigger revisiting it.

## Key Points

- **The compensating control is repository privacy,** not the secret's own validity — the secret remains live and usable by anyone who obtains the repo contents.
- **Recording the skip in `STATUS.md` is what makes it a decision.** An undocumented non-rotation is indistinguishable from not having noticed; the file the next session opens is where the distinction has to live.
- **Rotating mid-cutover would have added a second variable.** The secret exists in configuration on both machines, and the Windows leg was being decommissioned in the same session — a rotation would have to land on the Mac, on the retired Windows configuration, and in the vendor console simultaneously, while the pulls were the thing being verified.
- **Exposure and validity are independent axes.** The SpeedProfiling precedent is the sharper form of this: deleting a local Catapult token file did not revoke the token server-side, and manual revocation in the OpenField UI was a separate action.
- **Privacy is itself a revocable state.** The 2026-09-09 public-repo audit flipped 18 repositories private after finding real athlete data in two of them, which is direct evidence that "the repo is private" is a property that has been wrong before.

## Details

The useful discipline here is not the decision but its form. A credential deferral has two failure modes: rotating under time pressure and breaking a pipeline that was just verified, or quietly doing nothing and later being unable to distinguish a considered risk acceptance from an oversight. Writing "skip for now" with its reason into the repository's own `STATUS.md` addresses the second directly, and does so at the location a future reader of that repo will actually arrive at — the same placement logic that put the `pmset` undo command next to its enable command and that is generalized in [[connections/write-the-decision-where-each-consumer-will-look]]. The record also makes the risk model explicit and therefore contestable: the claim is that private-repo visibility is sufficient containment for this secret, which someone can now disagree with, rather than an unstated assumption nobody can see.

Where the deferral is weaker than its sibling is the absence of a revisit trigger. The sleep-lateness decision recorded in [[concepts/mac-owned-data-pulls-sleep-lateness]] was paired with a falsifiable condition — reconsider if GPS data goes *missing*, not merely late — which keeps the deferral from decaying into a permanent default. "Skip for now" names no such condition, so the natural trigger candidates (the repo ever becoming public, the secret appearing in a log or export, a vendor-side credential review, the next machine migration) remain unwritten. The cheap fix, consistent with the rest of this system's practice, is to attach either a condition or a verification date to the line, since a bare deferral is the one form of decision record that is indistinguishable from forgetting after enough time passes. The credential-consistency work on PR #1668, where load, save, remove, report, diagnose, and path resolution all had to route through a single credential store, is the companion lesson on the other side: once a secret is genuinely rotated, every code path that touches it must agree, which is part of why rotation is not a one-line action and why deferring it during a migration is a reasonable call.

# Fix From the Working Machine, Hand the Broken One a Paste-Ready Page

Facing a broken Windows backup that could only be *repaired* on Windows, the 2026-09-14 session chose to do as much of the work as possible from the Mac: edit the scripts, author the new manifest, and write a single instruction page for the Windows machine to follow. The stated rationale was that the edits are safe to make from the Mac, and doing so converts the eventual Windows session from a debugging job into one paste. The 2026-09-21 data-pull cutover applied the same split in its verification direction, reducing the Windows-side work to one command with an expected output.

## Key Points

- **The split is by what each machine can do, not by where the problem is.** File edits travel through the shared repos and were done on the Mac; only the operations that require the Windows machine's own scheduler (`Set-ScheduledTask`, admin PowerShell 7, a logged-in user session) were deferred.
- **The deliverable is an instruction page, not an executable.** The user asked twice for clarification on "the Windows file" — the wording was ambiguous about whether it was a script to run or a page to follow. Naming the artifact's *kind* is part of the handoff.
- **Verification can be handed over the same way.** On 2026-09-21 the Windows-side check was reduced to `git pull` plus `Select-String -Path refresh_all_data.bat -Pattern "skipped"` with an expected three lines — a one-paste task whose result the Mac-side session could interpret without seeing the machine.
- **A file that nothing reads yet is documented as such.** `backup-manifest.windows.json` records the real Windows destinations, with an explicit note inside the file that no checker consumes it — it is documentation until a Windows checker exists.
- **Two constraints were recorded as prohibitions:** do not move the scripts out of `DEV\_INBOX\` (the registered task points there), and do not re-enable the nine disabled tasks (their script is now the Mac's version).
- **Deferring the fix to "next time I'm on Windows" was the rejected alternative,** because it would have carried the whole diagnosis into a future session that would have to re-derive it.

## Details

The move generalizes beyond this incident. When two machines share a repository, the class of work that can be performed remotely is larger than it first appears: anything that is a file edit — scripts, configuration, manifests, instructions — can be authored from whichever machine the operator is currently sitting at, because the sync layer delivers it. What genuinely cannot be done remotely is narrow and identifiable: operations against the other machine's OS-level state, its scheduler, its mounted volumes, its running processes. Partitioning the work along that line front-loads all the thinking into the session that has the context and leaves the other machine a mechanical checklist. This is the same economy as the ten-section `docs/WINDOWS-SYNC.md` queue in [[concepts/dev-thin-repo-github-consolidation]], where the shared repo became a work channel between two machines that share no filesystem.

The 2026-09-21 cutover shows the pattern extending from repair to *confirmation*, which is the harder half. A remote verification step is only handable if its expected output is stated in advance; otherwise the receiving side must judge what it sees, which is the debugging work the pattern is trying to avoid. Marking the retired steps `skipped` rather than deleting them is what made that possible — it turned the question "is the cutover complete on Windows?" into a line count with a known answer of three (see [[concepts/decommissioned-leg-verified-by-skipped-markers]]). The general recipe is therefore: author the change from the working machine, and design the remote check so that it returns a value comparable against a number you have already written down.

The two documentation choices are what make the handoff durable rather than merely present. Writing "nothing reads this yet" *inside* `backup-manifest.windows.json` addresses the file's most likely future misreading — a maintainer finding a plausible manifest and assuming it is live, or finding it stale and assuming a checker broke. This is the same in-file rationale discipline that kept `CLAUDE.md` from being collapsed into an `@AGENTS.md` pointer, and that kept `DexaProject`'s permanent manifest warning from being repeatedly re-investigated: the explanation belongs in the file the next reader will open, not in a commit message. The two prohibitions serve the same function in reverse — they pre-empt the two most natural "tidying" impulses (move the scripts somewhere sensible; turn the disabled tasks back on), each of which would break something. The repeated clarification request about "the Windows file" is a small but real lesson about handoff wording: a path handed across a machine boundary is ambiguous between several kinds of artifact — a script to execute, a document to read, a config to install — and the receiving side cannot disambiguate from the filename.

# Connection: Write the Decision Where Each Consumer Will Look

## The Connection

The 2026-09-21 cutover closeout produced one handoff note and four `STATUS.md` updates. The handoff went to `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-09-21-mac-owns-data-pulls.md`; the per-repo records went into `DataBase_GPS_Reporting`, `PlayerProfiles_FB_03-28-2026`, `ForcePlate_DecisionSystem`, and `_INBOX`. Each repo got the part of the decision that its own future reader would need: the `pmset` enable *and* undo commands in the GPS repo whose schedule they govern, the VALD secret's "skip for now" in `_INBOX` where that configuration lives. This is the same instinct that put "nothing reads this yet" inside `backup-manifest.windows.json` rather than in a commit message.

## Key Insight

**A decision record's correct location is determined by how the next reader will arrive at the question, not by where the decision was made.** A central handoff directory is organized by session; a person hitting a problem is organized by repository — they open the project they are debugging, not the closeout note for the day the choice was made. So a single well-written handoff is necessary and insufficient: it preserves the narrative, but it is not on the path anyone will actually walk.

The corollary is that duplication across locations is correct here rather than sloppy, because the alternative is a pointer chain. A `STATUS.md` line saying "see the 2026-09-21 handoff" defers the answer to a second hop that can go stale — the exact failure documented in [[connections/a-stale-pointer-resolves-cleanly-to-the-wrong-answer]], where a pointer resolves successfully and returns the wrong thing. Writing the actual command or the actual rationale at each consumption point costs a few duplicated lines and removes the hop. The cost is the ordinary one of any duplication — divergence — which is why the fan-out should carry facts that are stable (a `pmset` incantation, a risk acceptance) rather than volatile ones (counts, current status), per [[connections/document-the-mechanism-not-the-magic-number]].

The third element is that a deferral needs this more than a completed action does. Finished work leaves its own evidence in the filesystem; a *non*-action leaves nothing at all, and an unrecorded non-action is indistinguishable from an oversight. Both of the day's deferrals — no `pmset` wake, no secret rotation — exist as decisions only because somebody wrote them into a file. The `pmset` case also shows the strongest form: store the undo alongside the enable, so reversing the decision requires no re-derivation regardless of which way it was settled.

## Evidence

- **2026-09-21 fan-out:** one handoff note plus `STATUS.md` updates in four repositories, each receiving the portion of the cutover relevant to it.
- **Paired enable and undo:** `sudo pmset repeat wakeorpoweron MTWRFSU 16:28:00` and `sudo pmset repeat cancel` both recorded in `DataBase_GPS_Reporting/docs/STATUS.md`, for a wake that was recommended on 9/21 and declined on 9/22 — the record survived the reversal.
- **Deferral recorded, not omitted:** "skip rotating the exposed VALD client secret — repo is private and pulls work," written as "skip for now" in `_INBOX/docs/STATUS.md`.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

Before scraping the same fields from several pages, first run `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset (or `firecrawl_find_tools`): a matching Alexandria provider returns those fields as typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: pass `alexandria` instead of `url`; the `alexandria` and `requestId` parameters describe batching, retries, errors and provider terms. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Alexandria execution ID. Reuse the returned ID for retries of the identical payload, never a new ID to bypass pending or uncertain execution; generated when omitted. For potentially large workflow results, supply and preserve one before execution. Errors relay a code and chargeId: request_in_flight (409) retry the same requestId later; request_unresolved (503) keep the requestId for reconciliation, never mint a new one; duplicate_request (409) the requestId belongs to a different payload; unknown_provider (404), insufficient_credits (402) and billing_unavailable (503) mean nothing executed.

alexandria.description: Execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities instead of scraping a URL. Exactly one of url or alexandria. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, found through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only timeout also applies at the top level. Read the selected contract before executing: required inputs and requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group), example.request/example.response when present, and response.key (do not assume records is the result key). Follow the declared pagination input and response cursor, preserving filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; check each item even when the outer response succeeds. If a response provides nextTool, follow it to read a large result instead of repeating a successful provider call. Needs an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. A terms-gated provider returns THIRD_PARTY_DATA_TERMS_REQUIRED (403) with requiresAction.url: follow the returned terms/show and terms/accept calls through this tool, accepting only after explicit user authorization for the reviewed version and digest; an organization admin can instead accept at the dashboard URL. Retry only after confirmed acceptance.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only, or sources: ["web"] for web only. domainTools: false disables domain matching. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. Execute a matched tool through firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body; use firecrawl_find_tools to browse the catalogue or read a full contract.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. Passing sources without alexandria in it (for example ["web"] or ["news"]) excludes Alexandria provider matches; omit sources unless you specifically need web-only or news-only results, or include "alexandria" alongside them. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
